If that doesn't exist, founders who just want to a get a new product, technology, or service out the door generally won't bother researching and developing equity and profit sharing models before they run out of money and have to accept external investment. An alternative organizational structure which I believe is worth exploring would be to continually create and issue 1 share per necessary labor hour completed, where the total number of shares in circulation is equal to the total number of labor hours completed by everyone who worked for the organization since its creation.

I think every company, corporation, business, charity, etc. should have a specific stated goal.

Currently, all goals are "Make money". They don't help people.

Well, ideally a general purpose goal of 'making money' would help the workers and make the workers of that organization better off, by allowing them to be compensated for making someone else better off, and improving the efficiency at which society allocates or transforms resources by offering a product or service which generates value for someone.

And it is also in the interest of workers to steer 'money making' in the direction of a stable, specialized, and reliable niche so that they are able to remain employed and any accrued shares they have acquired from their time spent at the organization retain their value in order to provide for a portion of their retirement.

But the problem is, without equity and profit sharing agreements, workers are not made better off, and are not able to steer the company towards that stable and specialized niche, especially if it's an older company which no longer possesses any original founders.

What I think we need is an organization structure somewhere in between that of a corporation and cooperative, so we have the drive for excellency in products, services, and efficiency, but where productive workers reap the benefits of making things more efficient and automated by gaining additional equity and a share of the profits. In the current structure, employees who are good at automating things and improving efficiency are not rewarded with equity and profits but with putting themselves out of a job.
